en: The Deeds of Harṣa; First Chapter.
Homage to him who is beautiful with the moon as a chowrie kissing his lofty head!
Salutations to Śambhu, the foundational pillar for the construction of the city of the three worlds.
I bow to Umā, whose eyes were closed in the bliss of embracing the throat of Hara,
appearing as if she had fallen into a swoon from contact with the Kālakūṭa poison.
Salutation to that Vyāsa, the omniscient creator of poets,
who fashioned the *Bhārata*, a source of merit, like the land of Bhārata fashioned by Sarasvatī.
For the most part, bad poets in this world—whose vision is dominated by passion—are born talkative and acting according to their whims, like the cuckoo. (1.4)
Like dogs, there are countless members of this breed in every house;
but poets who are true creators are not many, like śarabhas.
By changing various syllables and by concealing the marks of composition, a poet-thief is recognized among the virtuous even when his work remains unnamed. (1.6)
Among the Northerners, poetry consists primarily of wordplay; among the Westerners, it contains merely the sense;
among the Southerners, it is characterized by poetic fancy (utprekṣā); and among the Gauḍas, it is a clamor of syllables.
A novel theme, non-vulgar diction, unstrained punning, clear sentiment, and a composition of complex syllables—all these together are difficult to achieve in a single work. (1.8)
Of what use is the poetry of that poet whose speech— like the story of the Mahābhārata that encompasses all events— does not pervade the three worlds?
How could those lords of poets not be worthy of homage—those whose eloquence flows from their mouths even at the end of a breath, and who never grow weary? 1.10.
The pride of poets surely vanished because of the *Vāsavadattā*,
just as that of the sons of Pāṇḍu vanished when their spear came within the range of Karṇa.
The prose composition of Bhaṭṭāra Hariścandra, radiant with its arrangement of words, captivating, and maintaining the proper sequence of phonemes, acts as a king. 1.12.
Sātavāhana made this treasury imperishable and refined,
filling it with well-spoken words of pure origin, just as one fills a storehouse with gems.
The fame of Pravarasena, radiant as the white water-lily,
has reached the far shore of the ocean by means of a bridge, even as the army of monkeys.
Through plays composed by Sūtradhāra, which possessed many stages and were adorned with banners, Bhāsa attained fame, just as one does through temples.
Whose heart does not experience a deep and sweet delight upon encountering the eloquent verses of Kālidāsa, as if beholding clusters of blossoms thick with honey? (1.16)
Whom would the *Bṛhatkathā* not astonish? Illuminating the god of love and providing the adornments for Gaurī, it is like the playful sport of Śiva himself.
Even when the efforts undertaken by wealthy kings are remembered as being present in one's heart, the tongue feels as if it were being pulled inward and does not proceed toward poetry. (1.18)
Nevertheless, out of devotion to the King and fearing [the consequences], yet anxious about the conclusion,
I perform this restless lashing of my tongue upon the ocean of narrative.
The narrative shines like a bed adorned with golden jars, made delightful by its pleasant awakening and resplendent with the sounds of its expositions.

Victorious is Harṣa, who provides protection for the world with the rampart of his blazing fire of majesty, and who is a mountain of glory for the fulfillment of the desires of all his well-wishers. 1.21.

Thus it is heard: in ancient times, it is said, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, while presiding over his own world, sat upon a blossoming lotus-throne surrounded by the gods headed by Indra; he remained there at one time engaged in discourses on the Vedas and cultivating various other faultless assemblies for the discussion of knowledge.
As he sat there, worthy of being gazed upon by the three worlds, all the Prajāpatis—Manu, Dakṣa, Cākṣuṣa, and the rest—and the great Ṛṣis led by the Seven Sages attended upon him.
Some chanted the Ṛg-verses, skillful in praise; others recited the Yajus-formulas that bring honor.
Some sang the *sāmans* of praise;
others expounded the mantras whose ritual procedures and applications were laid open.
And there, disputes arose among them due to contradictions in their knowledge.

Then, Durvāsas by name— the son of Atri, brother of the Lord of Tārā, and a sage of great asceticism who was by nature exceedingly irascible— while quarreling with another sage named Mandapāla, became blinded by anger and sang out of tune while chanting the Sāman hymns.

And while all those sages remained silent out of fear of his curse, and while the Lotus-born Brahmā was treating him with indifference through the sport of engaging in conversation with others, [the sage continued].
The Blessed Virgin Kumārī, abiding in an age when childhood had slightly departed and fresh youth was adorned,
fanned the Grandfather with her creeper-like arms moving as they held a chowrie;
she shone with her two sprout-like feet, which were naturally ruddy yet appeared as if flushed with the passion born from her reprimanding him.

Her pair of feet was made resonant by a pair of anklets that jingled like two disciples reciting the *padapāṭha* and *kramapāṭha*; her two shanks bore the graceful appearance of the two pillars of the gateway to the City of Dharma;
and with the sprout-like palm of her left hand resting upon a girdle-string that warbled like the sweet, playful cries of a flock of swans.
Her body was sanctified by the sacred thread draped over her shoulder, which seemed as if it were the very collection of her virtues clinging to its residence in the minds of the learned;
she bore a necklace with a radiant central gem followed by many pearls, like the path to liberation (apavarga-mārga) accompanied by numerous liberated souls;
and she shone with a throbbing lip, rosy as if stained by the lac-dye of all the sciences that had entered her mouth.
She bore cheek-bosses that seemed like a reflection of the black antelope skin transferred from her lotus-seat, as if the deer of the moon had descended there to listen to her sweet singing;
with the creeper-like eyebrow raised slightly and askance in disdain,

she seemed to wash one ear— polluted by hearing the discordant notes— with a stream of tears flowing from the corner of her eye, while her other ear was adorned by a blossoming cluster of white Sindhuvara flowers.
As if laughing with manifest pride in her learning,
she was being attended by swarms of bees upon the flowers used as ear-ornaments— as if by *praṇavas* devoted to the Vedas;
her body was covered by a garment that was fine and pure, as if by the very expanse of her wisdom.
Scattering the moonlight of her teeth’ radiance in the ten directions like the pure essence of speech itself, the goddess Sarasvatī laughed upon hearing him.
Seeing her laughing in that manner, the sage said, “Ah! You evil-doer, you who are falsely conceited by a mere fragment of ill-grasped learning!”

Having said, "You mock me," he shook his head, causing the mass of his matted locks—whose binding was loosened by the shaking and which revealed a flickering tawny luster—to drench the ten directions as if with the liquid of the fire of his wrath.

With his forehead, darkened like a gaming-board and appearing as if the presence of Death had been summoned, he knit his brows into a crocodile-like frown that served as a decorative leaf-design for the inner apartments of the God of Death.
And with his exceedingly red eye, he seemed to offer a libation of his own blood to the Goddess of Indignation.
He seemed to arrest speech, which was fleeing in fear of his mercilessly bitten lips, under the guise of the luster of his teeth;
he appeared to be re-knotting his black antelope skin, which was slipping down, as if it were the very scroll of a decree of a curse;
and every limb of his was occupied by gods, demons, and sages who, reflected in his sweat, had sought refuge with him out of fear of the curse.

With a hand whose fingers were trembling with anger, he cast aside his rosary—which seemed like a string of syllables intended for propitiation—and having sipped water from his ascetic’s pitcher, he took up the water for the curse.

At that moment, seated near Svayambhū, there appeared the Goddess in embodied form, clad in the bark-garment of a *kalpa* tree that was as white as a mass of nectar-foam; her waist-knot was fastened between her high breasts with a silken cloth made of lotus fibers.
Her forehead was adorned with three lines of ash-marks that shone like the banners of victory over the three worlds conquered by the power of her asceticism;
she wore a sacred thread-like cloth (yogapaṭṭaka) white as the foam of nectar, hanging from her shoulder, which—coiled by the majesty of her penance—resembled the stream of the Gaṅgā;
and with her left hand, she held a crystal water-pot that looked like a lotus bud from which Brahmā had emerged.
Raising her right hand— which encircled a rosary, was bristling with bracelets fashioned from conch shells, and had its forefinger flickering in a threatening gesture—
she cried out, "Ah, you sinner, you who are struck down by anger!"
O evil-souled one, ignorant one,
selfless one!
O ignorant one,
O one who does not know the self, O wretched Brahmin!
O chief of sages, outcaste,
one who has been cast out!

"How is it that, abashed by your own transgression, you desire to curse the Blessed Goddess Sarasvatī— the Mother of the Three Worlds and the one worthy of worship by the hosts of gods, asuras, sages, and men?"—
so saying, they arrived with their mouths resonant with the syllable *Oṃ* from the cane seats cast off in anger, filling the quarters with the weight of their tossing masses of matted hair,

darkening the day with the expansive shadows of black antelope skins whirled during their circumambulations, and causing the world of Brahmā to tremble with the swaying vibrations of their sighs of indignation.

Sāvitrī rose from her grass mat together with the four Vedas in embodied form—those who, under the guise of trickling drops of *soma* juice, appeared to have foreheads smiling with the sacred ashes of the *agnihotra* sacrifice; who wore garments of *kuśa* grass fibers, yak-tail whisks, and bark rags; and who carried water-pots as their weapons.
Then she said, "Forgive me, O Blessed One."

Although he was entreated by the gods, saying, "This is no ground for a curse," and although he was being propitiated by his own disciples with joined palms, saying, "Preceptor, forgive this one lapse," [he replied,] "Son..."
Although he was being restrained by Atri with the words, "Do not create an obstacle to your asceticism," Durvāsas, overwhelmed by a fit of rage, said: "O ill-behaved woman!
I shall strip you of this pride born of your learning."
"Go down to the mortal world," he said, and released that curse upon her.
As Sāvitrī was about to pronounce a counter-curse, he said, "Friend,
restrain your anger."
"Even those whose minds are unconditioned are worthy of honor by virtue of their very birth as twice-born," saying this, Sarasvatī herself restrained her.
Then, seeing Sarasvatī thus cursed, the blessed Grandfather (Brahmā), wearing a body clad in a white sacrificial thread that resembled a lotus-fiber clinging to his place of birth,

silenced the clamor of the curse with his right hand— his hand which bore a cluster of rays from an emerald ring like a spreading creeper, and which appeared to hold a bundle of *kuśa* grass for quelling the calamities of the three worlds.

Casting, as it were, the initial lines for the commencement of the future Kṛta Yuga across the quarters with his exceedingly pure and long rays from his teeth, and filling the directions like an auspicious drum for the departure of Sarasvatī,
he spoke in a very firm voice: "Brahman,
this path is certainly not one frequented by the virtuous."
By means of that [path] upon which you have set out,
this [discipline] destroys the power of others;
for the dust raised by the horses of the unrestrained senses clouds the vision of those who have not conquered their senses.
Or to what extent does the eye perceive?
For those of perfected intellect see all objects—whether non-existent or existent—with a purified mind.
Moreover, the coexistence of righteousness and anger in a single place is as naturally opposed as that of water and fire.
Why do you abandon the light and plunge into darkness?
For forbearance is indeed the root of all asceticism.
Your intellect, like an angry vision skilled at perceiving the faults of others, does not see the fault of its own passion.
Where is the state of being a carrier of the great burden of majesty, and where is partiality?
A person who possesses sight but is excessively wrathful is truly blind.
An intellect clouded by anger does not discern what ought to be done or what ought not to be done;
for one who is angry, knowledge first becomes darkened, and only then does the frown appear.
In the beginning, passion assails the senses; at the end, the eye [fails]. At the outset, asceticism melts away.
Afterwards, the water of perspiration;
first the golden [armlet] throbs,
immediately thereafter the lower lip.

How is it that for the destruction of the world, you have produced matted hair and bark garments like those of a poisonous tree? Indeed, the state of your mind—round and polished like a string of pearls—is utterly unsuited to this ascetic garb.
Like an actor, you vainly wear the costume of a forest hermit with a heart devoid of true tranquility.
I do not see even the slightest bit of virtue in you;
because of this extreme deficiency, you still float only upon the surface of the ocean of knowledge.
Indeed, these great sages are certainly not deaf, mute, or blind, nor are they dull-witted.
"Since your own heart, which is the seat of the fault of anger, ought to have been restrained, why did you restrain the blameless Sarasvatī?
These are those very lapses of self-negligence and embarrassment because of which an undiscerning person becomes an object of reproach. Having said this, he spoke again: "Dear child Sarasvatī,"
Do not fall into despair;
this Sāvitrī shall follow you and will dispel the sorrow of our separation.
"And this curse of yours shall last until you behold the lotus-face of your own son.

Having said this much, he dismissed the assembly of gods, demons, sages, and men; then, placing his hand upon the shoulder of Nārada who had approached him in agitation, he rose to perform his customary daily rites.
Sarasvatī, too, being thus cursed, cast her gaze slightly downward upon her breast, which was like a streak of black antelope skin variegated with white and black.
She was being dragged along by swarms of bees that clung to the fragrance of her fragrant breath as if they were the embodied syllables of a curse;
with her face cast downward, she seemed to be suspending the path for descending to the mortal world, her hand having slackened from the grief of the curse;
and she was followed by flocks of domestic *kalahaṃsa* geese summoned by the tinkling of her anklets, as if they were the hearts of the inhabitants of Brahmaloka following her. Together—
She went home with Sāvitrī.
In the meantime, as if to announce the news of Sarasvatī’s descent, the sun, garlanded with rays, descended to the middle world.
And gradually, as the day waned, the lake became despondent at the calamity of its clusters of closing lotuses.

As the Lord, the sole eye of the world, descended with great speed from the mountain peak— reddened like the hair of a very young monkey and appearing as if cast down by the sidelong glances of amorous women arched with the frown of wine-intoxication—

the divine hermitages on their outskirts were whitened by the streams of milk flowing from the udders of the herd of Māheyī cows, as if washed by the waves of the Ocean of Milk at the rising of the moon.
And Airāvata, his tusks jingling from striking the golden slopes as he wandered about in the late afternoon, began to graze at leisure upon the banks of the celestial river.

The path of the stars manifests a rosy hue, as if smeared with the lac-dye from the feet of thousands of Vidyādhara women setting out on their trysts; while the quarters of the sky are colored by the sun’s setting-offerings presented by Siddhas traveling through the heavens,
the sky flows with the glow of safflower like the red sandalwood sap of the sweat of Twilight, who rejoices at being embraced by the wielder of the Pināka bow.

In the Brahma-world, which shines like a collection of all lotus-pools come to serve the lotus from which Brahmā was born, where the forests of hands joined in *añjali* by throngs of the most eminent sages offering salutations are being formed during the twilight prayers,
and where the *brahman* of the third *savana* is being chanted— within that *brahman*.

In the dwellings of the Seven Sages, where the courtyards were thick with the flames of kindled sacrificial fires as if they had begun the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) of their encampments for the performance of dharma; while the ascetics were rendered light and healthy, their sins and the poison of disease washed away by the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite; while the sandy banks were purified by rows of ascetics seated for the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*); while the lotus-born Brahmā’s vehicle, the swan, floated upon waves jagged with the laughter of his white plumage—acting as a parasol for the water-deities and a palace for the inner apartments of the wives of the birds; and while the night-lily grove, sweet with its own honey-scented fragrance, was about to rejoice, bringing delight to the bees.

When the flock of royal swans, delighted by drinking the sweet honey of the day-lotuses fading at the close of day, desired to sleep with their necks curved for the scratch of soft lotus stalks, fanning the lake of lotuses with the vibration of their wing-feathers; when the evening breeze—grey with the pollen of flowers from the creepers on the riverbanks, carrying the fragrance of jasmine from the braided hair of the city women of Siddhapura, thin and resembling the very breath of night—had begun to blow; and when the swarm of bees was resting within the hollows of the lotus buds, crowded with the tips of long filaments rising as they closed; [The passage continues... ...when the moon, the lord of the stars, had ascended the eastern mountain, appearing like a fresh leaf of the *mandāra* tree, white as a conch shell, its rays spreading like the fibers of a lotus stalk; when the sky, adorned with clusters of stars, resembled a pond filled with full-blown white lotuses; when the quarters of the world were whitened by the moonlight, appearing like a woman whose face is covered in a white veil; when the night had become cool and pleasant, with the heat of the sun’s rays dispelled; when the forest regions were illuminated by the moonlight, appearing like a grove of blooming white lotuses; when the world was enveloped in darkness, appearing like a dark blue cloth; when the moon, the friend of the night-lotuses, had risen high, dispelling the dense mass of darkness like a lion shaking off a thicket of black antelope fur; when the moon, the lord of the stars, had ascended the eastern mountain, appearing like a fresh leaf of the *mandāra* tree, white as a conch shell, its rays spreading like the fibers of a lotus stalk; when the night had become cool and pleasant, with the heat of the sun’s rays dispelled; when the forest regions were illuminated by the moonlight, appearing like a grove of blooming white lotuses; when the world was enveloped in darkness, appearing like a dark blue cloth; when the moon, the friend of the night-lotuses, had risen high, dispelling the dense mass of darkness like a lion shaking off a thicket of black antelope fur; when the moon, the lord of the stars, had ascended the eastern mountain, appearing like a fresh leaf of the *mandāra* tree, white as a conch shell, its rays spreading like the fibers of a lotus stalk; when the sky, adorned with clusters of stars, resembled a pond filled with full-blown white lotuses;
when the quarters of the world were whitened by the moonlight, appearing
When the host of stars, resembling a cluster of *kuṭaja* buds in the forest of Śiva’s matted locks tossed by his dance, was crowning the vault of heaven;
when the sky, copper-hued from the lingering twilight and dark as a black cloud with the luster of ripening palm-fruit rind, was closing the earth over;
and when the darkness, in its fresh youth, was most capable of rending the veil of the thickest gloom—he [appeared].
When the clusters of campaka buds serving as ear-ornaments for the maiden Night began to blossom amidst the multitude of lamps;
when the eastern quarter, pale with the lovely light of the slender rays of the moon, acted like a young sandbank on the banks of the dark Yamunā whose waters had subsided;

when the darkness—possessing the luster of a blue jay’s wing—was dissolving like the tresses of proud women, blackened by the mass of the moon’s rays as they grasped them, and appearing like a lake of blooming blue lotuses in full bloom.

When the Blessed One, the white-rayed moon, had risen— bearing a body red as the flush of dawn, like the wife of the Night holding her lower lip smeared with the blood dripping from her own deer slain by the multitude of sharp, harsh claws of the lion dwelling in the caves on the ridges of the Eastern Mountain—
and when the darkness was destroyed, as if washed away by streams of water from moonstones fallen from the mountain;
At the clear hour of evening, when the lunar orb was filling the ocean as if through a great conduit made of ivory— the conduit carrying the streams of milk flowing from Goloka—

Sāvitrī spoke tearfully to Sarasvatī, who sat with a vacant heart as if meditating on something: “Friend, before you, who are so skilled in giving instruction to the three worlds, my tongue falters even as it speaks.”

You surely know how perverse are the crooked workings of fate—unpleasant, difficult to overcome, and momentary—which, though occurring toward a virtuous person, are as devoid of courtesy as those directed at the wicked.

Even a single, causeless spark of insult falling from an unworthy person defiles the mind of even the most high-spirited. And like a tree being constantly drenched with the water of tears, even one that has lost its leaves sprouts again in a thousand ways.
The subtlest atoms of heat bring exhaustion even to a person of extreme delicacy, like a *mālatī* flower;
and even a minute affliction falling upon the great is sufficient for their torment, like a goad to elephants.
Furthermore, kinsmen are bound by the knots of the natural snare of affection, and one's birthplace is difficult to abandon.
The separation from beloved people is as heart-rending as the stroke of a saw;
you ought not to be thus.
Indeed, you are no ground for the sprouting of the poisonous thorns of sorrow.

Moreover, when past karma— whether auspicious or inauspicious— is powerful and stands as the presiding factor over the production of results, what occasion is there for sorrow in a wise man, whether that karma lies before him or behind him?
And how is it that these drops of tears, which are themselves inauspicious, defile your face—the unique lotus that brings auspiciousness to the three worlds? Enough of this!
Tell me now, which region of the earth do you wish to adorn?
In which meritorious region do you wish to set foot?
Which sacred fords (tīrtha) do you desire to grace?
Or in which blessed abodes of penance-groves do you wish to perform austerities?
This dear circle of friends, skilled in service and delicate from long acquaintance with playing together in the dust, is ready to descend to the surface of the earth.
And you, O King of Cedi, having no other refuge, from this moment forth resolve— in thought, word, and deed— to take refuge in Him who is the creator of all sciences,
the bestower of ultimate bliss, who has purified the gods and asuras with the dust of His feet, and who fashioned the ear-ornament for Lakṣmī by means of the sprout that produced the nectar.

“The God of gods, the preceptor of the three worlds, Tryambaka, will grant you relief from the sorrow of this curse in a very short time. Having been addressed thus, Sarasvatī, her eyes white with tears like pearls that had been released, replied: “Dear friend, The original Sanskrit text is: devadevaṃ tribhuvanaguruṃ tryambakam / alpīyasaiva kālena sa te śāpaśokaviratiṃ vitariṣyatīti / evamuktā muktamuktāphaladhavalalocanajalalavā sarasvatī pratyavādīt—“priyasakhi,
"Roaming with you, neither separation from the world of Brahmā nor the sorrow of the curse shall cause me any distress at all.
Only the bliss of serving the lotus-like feet of Kamala moistens my heart.
Moreover, you yourself know those abodes of dharma on earth, those places suitable for the attainment of *samādhi* and fit for yoga, where I may dwell. Having spoken thus, she ceased.
And she passed those nights with her eyes seemingly unblinking, kept awake by an inner agitation of longing.

On another day, when the Blessed One, the crest-jewel of the three worlds, had risen; when the crest-jewel of the Eastern Mountain shone forth, its body reddened as if by the blood shed from the mouths of his own horses as they stumbled and bit their bridles with a *khaṇa-khaṇa* sound; and when it was preceded by the deep red crests of aged cocks.

Not far away, the protector of the swan-flock, surveying the celestial chariot of his grandfather as he wandered about, sang aloud in the *aparavaktra* meter: "O female swan, cherished by your dwelling in a mind that is pure yet longing, why do you cause your gaze to tremble?
Descend to the pond; you shall return once more to your home among the lotuses."
Having heard that, Sarasvatī thought again: "I have been questioned by him just as I myself was. Very well;
I shall honor the sage's word. Having said this, she rose, resolved to descend to the surface of the earth, and abandoned her grief-stricken separation.

Disregarding her own attendants and circle of kinsmen, she circumambulated the Four-faced One three times; then, having somehow persuaded him to turn back the throng of following ascetics, she departed from the world of Brahmā accompanied by Sāvitrī.
Thereafter, she proceeded gradually like the celestial cow Dharmadhenu, with her white udders flowing downward.
Resounding with a loud roar,
bearing a garland of *mālatī* flowers upon the head of the slayer of Andhaka,
its banks crowded by the settling *bālakhilya* sages;

The river had its banks washed by Arundhatī with the bark of *tāra* trees; its shimmering, high-arching waves caused its bright stars to tremble; its sandy shores were made to bristle with the liquid offerings of sesame seeds bestowed by ascetics; its further banks were whitened by the funeral cakes offered to the ancestors by Pitāmaha after he had purified himself by bathing; and it indicated the fast observed during the birth-impurity of the Sun by the beds of *kuśa* grass where the Seven Sages slept upon its banks.
It was variegated by heaps of flowers released for worship from the hands of Indra, purified by sipping water; it bore the discarded *nirmālya* garlands of Mount Mandara fallen from the city of Śiva;
and it shattered the rocks within the caves of Mandara with its disdainful force.
Her body was caressed by the jar-like breasts of a multitude of beautiful women who desired her;
her current was made resonant by the stumbling of crocodiles and boulders;
and her banks were starred with clusters of spray from the nectar of the moon dripping through the *suṣumṇā* channel.
Its sandy banks were grey with the smoke from the sacrificial fires of the *dhiṣaṇas*;
its *vidyādharas* fled in terror at the sight of the sand-lingas fashioned by the *siddhas* being stepped over;
it was like the slough cast off by the serpent of the sky.
It was like a playful forehead-mark for the king of heaven,
a marketplace for the merchandise of merit,
and a bolt fastened across the gateway to the city of hell.
Like a silken turban-band for King Sumeru,
like a silken palanquin-pole for the elephant that is Kailāsa,
and like a path to liberation;
Following Mandākinī, the queen of the seven-peaked mountain, as if she were the rim of the Kṛta Age, she descended to the world of mortals;
and even while remaining in the vault of the sky, she beheld [the river] like the necklace of Varuṇa,
and like a stream of nectar from the Moon-mountain.
Like a flow from the moonstones of the Vindhya mountains,
like a stream of resin from the camphor trees of the Daṇḍaka forest,
like a fountain of the essence of beauty from the quarters of the world;

Beholding that great river named Hiraṇyavāha— which people call the Śoṇa, which was filled with clear, cool, and delicious water, and which was like a crystal stone slab serving as a couch for the splendor of the sky— the daughter of the Lord Pitāmaha,
her heart captivated by its loveliness, made her dwelling upon its very bank.

And Sāvitrī said: "Friend, these regions on the banks of this great river—which has surpassed the splendor of the Mandākinī—delight me; for here the cries of sweet-voiced peacocks resound, the bases of the trees are strewn with sand from the masses of flower-pollen, and they are made charming by the humming of swarms of bees intoxicated by fragrance, which sounds like the music of flutes and lutes."
"And my heart is partial toward staying right here," he said.
His words being welcomed, she agreed, saying "So be it," and they alighted on its western bank.

"fortunate" depends on you;
and "constant affection" is a skillful proposal.
"To know how to serve" is the talk of one who is not his master; "to wish to remain in the state of a slave until death" is the speech of a rogue; "be the mistress of the house" is a mere lure.
"A fortunate woman serves such a husband"—this is partiality toward her master;
"you are his death"—this is unpleasant;
"you are ignorant of virtues"—this is an insult.
That she has shown him much favor even in his dreams is beyond witness;
that he entreats her for the sake of saving his life is cowardice;
and that she commands him to go there is [the height of] authority.
"Even when restrained, he comes by force; thus there is humiliation.
Therefore, having heard that 'you are beyond the reach of words, the Queen is the authority,' she became silent.
Then Sarasvatī replied with eyes wide with joy: "O friend,"
"I am unable to speak much more;
I stand here, O speaker of smiles, at your word.
Let these life-breaths be taken."
"But as for Mālatī, O Queen," she said, "I shall do as you command;
this is a great favor. Having spoken thus, overcome by intense joy, she prostrated herself and crossed the Śoṇa river on a swift horse.
She went to Cyavana’s hermitage to bring Dadhīca;
meanwhile, out of affection for her friend, she informed Sāvitrī as well of what had transpired.
Bearing the weight of longing and with a weary heart, she somehow passed the remainder of the day, which felt like an entire aeon.
And when the Lord of Rays had set,
as the darkness descended more intensely,
Sarasvatī spoke while the moon— white as if laughing, like a lion releasing a cave— was emerging from the eastern quarter.
Seated upon the red sand of the Śoṇa river— which was pure, more delicate than Chinese silk, and rippled like a soft bed of fine linen—
she sat with her prayer made in a dream; she wore upon her forehead a tilaka that seemed like the moonlight from the toenails of Dadhīca clinging there as he prostrated himself at her feet,
while the reflection in the mirror of her cheek addressed her as "O sweet-smiling one."

With her hand—whose circle of radiating nail-rays seemed like a mass of crescent moons turned into a fly-whisk—she fanned her perspiring cheek as if the moon itself were whispering Madana’s message into her ear, saying, "This person, the beloved of your heart, has been brought here.
She held across [the doorway] what appeared to be a playful cane-staff cast there by the God of Love, with the command: "No one is to enter here except Dadhīca."
Making her breasts resound with the sound of her tender lotus-stalk-like arms, she somehow bore herself in her heart and waited;
and this thought arose in her mind: "Even I, Sarasvatī, though knowing full well, have been brought under the sway of this mind-born god; what then can be said of other poor, fickle young women?"
And he arrived like the month of Madhu, bearing fragrant breezes; like a swan, possessing the grace of a lotus stalk; and like a peacock, with its face upturned in joy at the clouds.
With his slender body, white as fresh sandalwood paste, trembling like a Malaya breeze,
he was as if being dragged by the Lord of Planets who had seized him by the hand,
and as if being impelled by the southern wind, which is skilled at kindling the god of love.
With his slender body covered as if by a blue garment by a swarm of bees attracted by the fragrance— a swarm that was like a surge of the essence of passion,

full of longing— and with the interior of one cheek whitened by the reflection of the moon shimmering within him, which resembled the conch-shell of an elephant in rut intoxicated by love and seemed like a bashful smile from the first play of their union, [he stood] accompanied by Mālatī.
Dadhīca,

having arrived and conversed with a voice faltering like that of a swan— blended as it were with the sound of the anklets of his beloved dwelling in his heart— acted in accordance with what Love commands and what Youth instructs.
Just as cleverness instructs and passion teaches,
so did he delight that charming Rāmā.
Having conceived confidence in him, Sarasvatī disclosed her identity to him;
and with him, she passed more than a year as if it were but a single day. Then, by the turn of fate, Sarasvatī became pregnant.

And in no long time, she gave birth to a son who was delightful with every auspicious mark. To him, as soon as he was born, she granted a boon, saying: "By my power, all the Vedas along with their secret Upanishads, all the Śāstras, and all the arts shall manifest themselves spontaneously.

Then, as if to demonstrate her praise for her noble husband by taking Dadhīca within her heart, she ascended once more to the world of Brahmā together with Sāvitrī, following the command of the Grandfather.

When she had departed, Dadhīca, as if struck in his heart by the thunderbolt itself, entrusted the daughter of a sage named Akṣamālā—the wife of a Brāhmaṇa brother born of the Bhārgava lineage—to the care of his own son for the child’s upbringing; then, distressed by separation, he went to the forest to perform austerities.
At the very moment that Sarasvatī gave birth to a son, Akṣamālā likewise gave birth to a son.
She, however, gradually nurtured those two infants without distinction, providing them equally with breast milk and other nourishment.
Of the two, one was named Sārasvata, and the other was named Vatsa.
And between those two, there was a mutually enviable affection, like that of twin brothers.

Then Sārasvata, by the power of his mother, had at the very onset of youth manifested the entire collection of all branches of knowledge; he transmitted the entirety of the world of speech (*vāṅmaya*) to that beloved brother, his dear friend as dear as life, his child.
And out of affection, he established for him— a man who had taken a wife— a residence named Prītikūṭa in that very same region;
he himself, however,
remained an ascetic wearing matted hair and a black antelope skin.
Wearing a rosary of beads, clad in bark garments, and girt with a belt.
Having become a matted-haired ascetic, he went into the presence of his father, who was engaged in penance; then,
as Vatsa grew up, there arose a great exaltation of spirit in the people,
accompanied by a loud proclamation.
Borne upon the head of the Supreme Lord,
profound with all the scriptures of the arts,
and honored by the great sages.

A stainless lineage, capable of withstanding the agitation of opposing forces, having gained its future course upon the surface of the earth, and flowing without faltering like the current of the Bhāgīrathī, began to proceed, purifying all.

From whom were born those sages known as the Vātsyāyanas, who, though human, were like sages; who, though adhering to the Vedas, did not resort to the false chatter of herons and crows; and who, though observing the vow of the cock, did not possess the conduct of cats.
They had abandoned the company of worldly people;
they had avoided hypocrisy, the pretense of asceticism, and deceitful intentions; and they were free from the snares of secret intrigues.
Those who have humbled their own baseness,
whose natures are serene, and whose perversions are destroyed.
Their mental dispositions were turned away from censuring others;
their food was purified by abstaining from the three types of meat;
and they were steadfast and free from dejection.
They have shaken off all entreaties, their nature is free from treachery, and they are devoted to those who bow before them in supplication.
They had stilled all doubts concerning other scriptural branches and unraveled the knots of the meaning of every text;
they were poets and eloquent speakers.
Free from envy,
devoted to the eloquent sayings of others,
and possessing refined discernment regarding wit and humor.
They were skilled in hospitality, hospitable to all guests,
and esteemed by all virtuous people.
Their hearts were moistened by a flow of affection common to all sentient beings;
likewise, endowed with every virtue, they were not overcome by royal armies;
they possessed forbearance and were a source of joy for those who took refuge in them.
The Vidyādharas were not without swords;
they were not dull-witted, but possessed of artistic skill; and the stars were free from blemish.
They do not oppress others, yet they are radiant; they are without heat, yet they consume offerings; they are without guile, yet they possess coils.
They were pillars of virtue, abodes of merit; they were skillful, never failing in their ritual duties; they were free from malice, having conquered desire.
The twice-born are unique;
while they are thus being born and transmigrating within cyclic existence, [this occurs].
As the ages passed,
as the Kali age descended, and as the years rolled on,
As the days passed and time went by,
while the illustrious Vātsyāyana lineage was continuously flourishing through a succession of births,
there was eventually born a Brahmin named Kubera, who, like the bird Vainateya, took great pride in his noble ancestry.

To him were born four sons—Acyuta, Īśāna, Hara, and Pāśupata—who, like the beginnings of the four ages, caused the expansion of progeny through the power of Brahmā; who, like the arms of Nārāyaṇa, brought joy to the circle of the virtuous;

and among them, Pāśupata had a single son named Arthapati, who was as firm as the mountain range that supports the burden of the earth, as deep as the four oceans, and the crest-jewel of the entire circle of the foremost of the twice-born. He was a great-souled man.

He begot eleven sons— Bhṛgu, Haṃsa, Śuci, Kavi, Mahīdatta, Dharma, Jātavedas, Citrabhānu, Tryakṣa, Mahīdatta, and Viśvarūpa— who were like the eleven Rudras, pure and with faces sprinkled by droplets of the nectar of Soma.
And among them, Citrabhānu obtained a son named Bāṇa through a Brāhmaṇa woman named Rājadevī.
While still a child, he was separated from his mother by the power of a forceful destiny;
yet his father, having conceived an even deeper affection for him, assumed the role of a mother for him. And so he grew up in his own home, receiving even greater support and care from him.

When he had completed the entire cycle of rites beginning with the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and had returned home, his father— who was about fourteen years old— performed all the meritorious duties appropriate for the twice-born as prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and then passed away in due time before reaching his tenth year.
Upon the death of his father, overcome by great sorrow and with a heart burning day and night, he somehow managed to pass several days remaining within his own house.
And as his grief gradually thinned out— due to the inherent nature of independence to be a source of indiscipline, the abundance of curiosity characteristic of childhood,
and the fact that the onset of youth is the adversary of fortitude—
Performing many frolics appropriate for childhood, he became restless;
and he had friends and companions of his own age who were like him.
And so it was:
The two brothers Pāraśava, Candrasena, and Mātṛṣeṇa;
Bhāṣākadirīśāna, his supreme friend; and the two affectionate ones, Rudra and Nārāyaṇa.

The learned ones were Vārabāṇa and Vāsabāṇa; Varṇaka was the author of the *Veṇī*, the son of Bharata was the author of Prākṛta works, and Kulaputra was the author of the *Vāyuvikāra*; Bandin was the author of the *Anaṅgabāṇa*, and Sūcībāṇa was the other.
Katyanikā Cakravākikā,
Jāṅgulika Mayūraka, Kalāda Cāmīkara, and Hairika Sindhuṣeṇa.
The scribe is Govindaka, the painter is Vīravarman,
and the bookbinder is Kumāradatta.
Jīmūta was the drummer, Somila and Grahāditya were the singers,
and Kuraṅgikā was the female attendant.
The two flute-players were Madhukara and Pārāvata; the teacher of music was Darduraka; and there was a female masseuse.
The Kerala dancer was a young performer of the *tāṇḍava*,
Ākṣika was Ākhaṇjala, and Kitava was Bhīmaka.
The young actor Śikhaṇḍaka,
the dancer Hariṇikā,
and the mendicant Sumati.
The Jaina mendicant Vīradeva,
the storyteller Jayasena,
and the Śaiva Vakraghoṇa.
Karāla was a practitioner of mantras; Lohitākṣa was addicted to the subterranean openings of the asuras; and Vihaga was a master of the alchemy of base metals.
Dāmodara was a frog-catcher, Cakīrākṣa was a magician,
and Tāmracūḍaka was a wandering mendicant.

Followed by these and others, he— driven by childishness toward a life of dissipation, his heart captivated by the curiosity to see other lands— departed from his home despite the wealth inherited from his father and grandfather that was suitable for a Brahmin, and despite his unbroken pursuit of learning.
Unrestrained as if possessed by a demon, and led astray by the mind of fresh youth, he became an object of ridicule to the great men.
Then,

gradually and slowly, beholding the vast royal palaces that captivate the heart with their most noble conduct, and attending upon the preceptors' households illuminated by faultless learning, he proceeded.
Attending upon assemblies of conversation that were profound and endowed with highly precious qualities,
and plunging into circles of the learned whose intellects were naturally deep and rich, he once again returned to that very same wise and natural disposition befitting his own lineage.
After a long time, he returned once more to that very hermitage of the Vātsyāyana lineage, his own birthplace and the dwelling of Brahmins.

There, his arrival was greeted like a day of festival by trusted kinsmen whose affection had been renewed by their long absence and who revealed their kinship through their familiarity; seated in the midst of a circle of childhood friends, he experienced a bliss akin to liberation.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Vātsyāyana," in the *Harṣacarita* composed by the great poet Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
